records.name: SSO sign-in attempt and validation
records.description: User arrives on the Riverside marketing landing (hero) and moves into the authentication flow to access the product. Entry point: marketing homepage (user not signed in). The user clicks the site sign-in CTA which opens a credential modal. From the modal the user chooses Single Sign-On (SSO). The SSO flow presents an email entry field; the user enters an email address and submits. Exit points: successful SSO handoff (not shown) or an SSO validation error (shown). Assumptions: user is unauthenticated, using a desktop browser, and has access to standard sign-in methods displayed (social, email/password, SSO).
records.problem: Task the user is trying to accomplish: sign into their Riverside account using their organization's Single Sign-On (SSO) rather than a local email/password or social provider. From the user perspective they expect a clear path from marketing → sign-in → choose SSO → enter work email → be redirected to their identity provider or receive guidance if SSO isn't available for that email. From the interface/system perspective the UI must: present sign-in options, offer an SSO-specific entry path, accept an email input, validate whether that email is eligible for SSO, and surface a clear error if the address isn't recognized for SSO. Result at the end: user-perceived outcome — the user learns whether their email is accepted for SSO and either proceeds to SSO handoff or sees a helpful error message. System-level outcome — the platform attempts an SSO lookup/validation for the provided email and returns either a redirect instruction (to the IdP) or an error state explaining SSO is not configured for that address.

records.name: SSO email check and error handling
records.description: Entry: public marketing homepage (user is logged out). The user chooses to sign in and is routed to an email-first Single Sign-On (SSO) entry screen. The SSO screen requires only an email address and a Continue button; submitting the email triggers a check for SSO entitlement for that account. In the provided screenshots the check returns a negative result and the UI surfaces an inline error banner: "Your account is not configured to use SSO" and the user is offered a link to "Log in without SSO." Exit points: successful SSO redirect (not shown), or fallback to non-SSO login via the provided link. Assumptions: desktop viewport, user is unauthenticated, user attempts enterprise/SSO sign-in using an email address.
records.problem: User task: Sign in using an organizational SSO credential. From the user perspective they want a quick, familiar sign-in by entering their work email and continuing to their organization’s identity provider. They expect the system to detect whether their account is on an SSO-enabled domain and either forward them to the identity provider or explain next steps if SSO is not available. From the interface perspective the UI enables an "email-first" SSO check: a single input for email + Continue, minimal copy that communicates SSO intent, and a visible fallback link to the non-SSO login. The result in the happy path is a redirect to the identity provider (user-perceived outcome) and an authentication handoff on the server (system-level outcome). In the shown unhappy path the user sees an error banner stating their account is not configured for SSO (user-perceived), and the system has returned a negative SSO configuration check (system-level).

records.problem:

The system provides toast/error feedback if Save is attempted with no actual changes, shows a notice when custom commands changed, and triggers a workspace rebuild after a successful save (workspace status transitions, e.g., to "Building").

Result at the end:
- User-perceived outcome: The user sees confirmation that changes were saved (or an informative error if nothing changed) and then observes the workspace status update to "Building", indicating the system is applying the new configuration.
- System-level outcome: Workspace metadata (environment variables and setup commands) are updated on the server. If setup commands changed, the workspace template is rebuilt and a rebuild process is started (reflected by the workspace status change).

records.problem:
User task (user perspective): Remove an existing recovery code so it can no longer be used for account recovery. The user expects a clear, safe flow that prevents accidental deletion: a tooltip/confirmation prompt, a warning modal, and a verification step (code entry) with an option to resend. The user expects the UI to update to show the code is removed.

Interface/system perspective: The UI presents a list of recovery codes and an affordance to add a new one. When the user chooses delete, the UI shows an inline affordance (tooltip) and a destructive warning modal requiring explicit confirmation before proceeding. After confirming the modal, the system sends a verification code and requires the user to enter it in segmented input fields; a Delete button is disabled until the code is entered. On successful verification, the system removes the recovery code from the persisted list and returns the user to the Account Recovery list with a success state (the removed code no longer appears).

Result: User-perceived outcome — the selected recovery code is gone from the list and deletion felt deliberate and reversible only via re-creation. System-level outcome — the recovery-code record is deleted (or flagged as inactive) and the account's recovery options are updated accordingly.

records.name: Disable two-factor authentication
records.description: Happy path: A logged-in user opens their Personal Settings → Security section, clicks the control to disable two-factor authentication, verifies the change by entering either a time-based authenticator code or a recovery code in a modal, and then confirms. The system validates the code, disables 2FA for the account, and shows a success toast while toggling the control to the disabled state. Entry point: Personal Settings (Security). Exit point: Personal Settings with 2FA disabled and a confirmation toast. Assumptions: user is authenticated, has permission to change their own security settings, and has access to an authenticator app or one-time recovery codes; flow shown on a desktop browser.
records.problem:
Task: User wants to disable two-factor authentication (2FA) for their account.

User perspective:
- Goal: Remove the requirement to use an authenticator app when signing in.
- Decisions/expectations: The user expects a verification step (enter an authenticator code or a recovery code) to prevent accidental disabling, immediate confirmation that 2FA was disabled, and the security control to reflect the new state.

Interface/system perspective:
- What the UI enables: The Personal Settings page exposes a control to disable 2FA when it is currently enabled. Clicking that control opens a modal that requires entry of a two-factor code or a recovery code. The Save/confirm button is disabled until a code is entered. On valid code submission the UI shows a success toast and updates the Security section to show 2FA is disabled and replace the disable-control with an enable-control.
- What the UI enforces: A verification step (code input) is mandatory to proceed; the modal prevents further interaction with the underlying page until the modal is dismissed or completed.

Result at the end:
- User-perceived outcome: The user sees a success toast indicating 2FA is disabled and the Security section shows an "Enable 2FA" action instead of "Disable two-factor authentication." The user understands they will no longer need the authenticator app when signing in.
- System-level outcome: The account's two-factor authentication status is updated to disabled and the system will stop prompting for 2FA on subsequent sign-ins.

They expect clear warnings about irreversibility, alternatives (disable notifications or change profile URL), an opportunity to provide a reason, and a final confirm step. After confirmation the system should deactivate the account, schedule permanent deletion, and display a message with timeline and an option to log back in to cancel. End result: user-perceived outcome — the user sees a clear confirmation that their account has been deactivated and will be permanently deleted in 30 days with instructions to log in to cancel. System-level outcome — the account is marked deactivated and a deletion process/scheduler is set for 30 days; the session is ended or redirected to login.

The account settings experience allows the user to select a reason, review the consequences of deactivation, explicitly confirm understanding, and submit optional feedback before completing the request.
